analysis.one_liner: Restores federal pre-approval for states with recent records of voting discrimination before they change election rules.
analysis.headline: With all 218 cosponsors being Democrats, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a markup or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would restore the part of the Voting Rights Act that required certain states to get advance federal approval — from the Justice Department or a federal court — before changing their election rules. It sets a new formula: a state is covered for 10 years if it had enough voting-rights violations in the previous 25 years, and it also requires federal pre-approval for specific changes like stricter voter ID, fewer polling places, and certain redistricting plans in areas with sizable minority populations. It also requires public notice of voting changes and gives the Justice Department new tools to investigate.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters — especially Black, Latino, Asian American, Native American, and language-minority voters — in states and counties with recent records of voting-rights violations. They would regain a front-end safeguard: election rules that would dilute their vote could be blocked before taking effect, rather than challenged one lawsuit at a time after the fact. Voters everywhere in covered areas would also get new public-notice rights about polling place changes and redistricting.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters in areas with discrimination records

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new coverage formula so states and counties with 25-year records of voting-rights violations must preclear election changes with the Justice Department or a federal court for 10 years [S2].

Requires pre-approval for specific practices, including stricter voter ID or proof-of-citizenship requirements, cuts to polling locations or voting hours, reduced multilingual materials, and certain redistricting changes in jurisdictions where minority groups make up a significant share of the population [S3].
Restores the vote-dilution and vote-denial legal standards courts use, and makes it easier for voters to get fast court relief before an election rather than after the ballots are cast [S3].
Requires states and counties to publicly notify voters within 48 hours of changes to voting rules and to disclose polling place resources and demographic data for redistricting changes [S3].
Lets the Justice Department demand documents and written answers from states to investigate voting discrimination before filing suit [S2].

analysis.who_pays: States, counties, and other local election authorities — particularly those with records of violations — would bear the cost of federal review before changing election rules, plus new notice and reporting duties. State legislatures and officials would lose the ability to change election laws without federal sign-off. The Justice Department's workload would grow.

drawbacks.text: Federal pre-approval shifts power over election rules from state governments to the Justice Department and a single federal court; critics argue this is an unusual federal intrusion into how states run elections and that a formula keyed to past violations permanently singles out certain states [S3].

Covered practices cannot take effect until the Justice Department declines to object within 60 days or a court approves them, which can delay election-law changes even when they are ultimately allowed [S3].

The bill expands the bases on which a state is deemed 'covered' to include Attorney General objections and settlements — not only final court judgments — which state officials argue can keep a jurisdiction covered based on contested or negotiated outcomes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: after the Supreme Court struck down the old coverage formula in 2013, voters could only fight discriminatory election rules through slow, case-by-case lawsuits after the harm occurred, and this bill restores a front-end check targeted at jurisdictions with recent records of violations. The costs are real too — less state control over election administration, federal review delays, and a formula that some states will fairly object to as based on decades-old conduct. On balance the bill is designed to be triggered by documented violations rather than geography alone, which addresses the constitutional problem that sank the old formula, but it would still concentrate significant power over elections in the executive branch.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee on September 19, 2023, and the committee never took it up, so it never came to a vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 19, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in its action history for the remainder of the 118th Congress [S5].
All 218 cosponsors were Democrats, giving the bill support from a numerical majority of the House but no Republican cosponsors [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee and would need to be reintroduced to advance.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State legislatures, county election officials, and political actors who want freedom to change election rules without federal pre-approval are better off that the bill never advanced. Voters in covered jurisdictions keep the status quo: no advance federal review, and protection only through lawsuits after a rule takes effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officials who change election rules unreviewed

for.name: Terri Sewell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 218 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including the full Democratic leadership slate (Jeffries, Clark, Aguilar, Clyburn, Pelosi and others)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from a numerical majority of the House.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill during the 118th Congress, leaving it without a path to the floor.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor and committee agenda
against.what_they_did: Brought no Republican cosponsors to the bill and never scheduled it for a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 218 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on; with Republicans controlling the House and its committee agendas, the bill never advanced past the referral.

industries.industry: State legislatures and state/local election officials
industries.note: The bill would require pre-approval before changing election rules in covered jurisdictions and impose new public-notice and reporting duties. Their interest in changing election rules without federal review runs against voters' front-end protections against discriminatory rules.

industries.industry: Political parties and campaign organizations operating in covered states
industries.note: Redistricting plans and election-rule changes that consolidate one party's advantage would face federal preclearance in jurisdictions with violation records, making it harder to lock in district maps drawn to dilute minority voting strength.

The bill adds causes of action, easier preliminary relief, and attorney's-fee coverage, expanding the work available to groups that challenge discriminatory voting rules. Their winning generally means voters keep access to the ballot.
